mcq.q: During a recession with high unemployment, an appropriate fiscal policy is to:
options: Cut government spending and raise taxes
Increase government spending and/or cut taxes
mcq.explain: An expansionary fiscal policy raises aggregate demand by increasing government spending or reducing taxes, which helps output and employment recover. Cutting spending and raising taxes would deepen the recession. Changing the repo rate and CRR are monetary policy tools of the RBI, not fiscal measures.
mcq.topic: Types of fiscal policy — expansionary and contractionary
mcq.fast: Recession -> expansionary fiscal policy (G up, T down).

mcq.q: Progressive income taxes and unemployment benefits reduce fluctuations without any fresh government decision. They are called:
mcq.explain: Automatic stabilisers work on their own: in a boom, incomes rise and tax collections rise faster under progressive taxes, restraining demand; in a recession, tax collections fall and benefit payments rise, supporting demand. Discretionary measures, by contrast, need deliberate new decisions by the government.
mcq.fast: Works without a new decision = automatic stabiliser.

mcq.q: Heavy government borrowing pushes up interest rates and reduces private investment. This is called:
options: Deficit financing by the central bank
mcq.explain: When the government borrows heavily from the market, it competes with private borrowers for limited savings, pushing interest rates up. Some private investment becomes unprofitable and is dropped, so government spending partly displaces private spending. This is crowding out, a limitation of fiscal policy.
mcq.topic: Limitations of fiscal policy and crowding out
mcq.fast: Govt borrowing squeezes private investment = crowding out.

mcq.q: Which of these is a limitation of fiscal policy?
options: Time lags in recognising the problem, deciding and implementing measures
It can never affect aggregate demand
It is controlled by the central bank
It has no effect on income distribution
mcq.explain: Fiscal policy suffers from recognition, decision and implementation lags, so measures may take effect after conditions have changed. Political pressures and crowding out are other limitations. It does affect aggregate demand and income distribution, and it is controlled by the government, not the central bank.
mcq.topic: Limitations of fiscal policy and crowding out
mcq.fast: Fiscal policy weakness = lags + politics + crowding out.

mcq.q: To control demand-pull inflation, the government should follow a:
options: Contractionary fiscal policy — lower spending and/or higher taxes
mcq.explain: Demand-pull inflation arises when aggregate demand exceeds what the economy can produce. A contractionary fiscal policy reduces aggregate demand by cutting government spending or raising taxes, easing pressure on prices. Higher subsidies and tax cuts would add to demand and worsen inflation.
mcq.topic: Types of fiscal policy — expansionary and contractionary

mcq.q: Which fiscal measure directly helps to reduce inequality of incomes?
options: A uniform lump-sum tax on everyone
Progressive taxation combined with welfare spending on the poor
mcq.explain: Progressive taxation takes a larger share of higher incomes, and the revenue can finance welfare schemes, education and health for the poor. Together they narrow income gaps. A uniform lump-sum tax and higher taxes on essentials fall more heavily on the poor, and cutting education spending would widen inequality.
mcq.topic: Fiscal policy for long-run growth and for reducing inequality
mcq.fast: Equity tools = progressive tax + pro-poor spending.

mcq.q: A government finances part of its deficit by borrowing from the central bank, which creates new money. The main risk is:
options: Crowding out through higher interest rates only
mcq.explain: When the central bank lends to the government by creating new money, the money supply increases. If output does not rise as fast, more money chases the same goods and prices rise. That is why monetised deficit financing is regarded as inflationary and is now restricted in India.
mcq.topic: Public debt and the budget as instruments
mcq.fast: Printing money to fund deficits -> inflation risk.
